newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians fear outcome of Jewish housing plan.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians fear outcome of Jewish housing plan.

text.p: Israeli policemen burst out of two vans that roared into an Arab neighbourhood in East Jerusalem on Wednesday, took up positions on its main street and squeezed the triggers of unloaded guns.
A day after Israeli municipal authorities in Jerusalem approved plans to build 132 homes for Jews in Ras al-Amoud, police began practising for urban warfare in the ramshackle area.
A Jerusalem police spokesman said he had no information about the drill witnessed by neighbourhood residents and a Reuters correspondent.

"They have not built anything yet and you see what they are doing," said Mahmoud Qassem, 62, a Palestinian grocer, while watching the police take mock aim and then pile back into the vans and drive away.
"If they build this settlement, it will be like putting a gas tank next to a flame," he said.
The Jerusalem District Planning Commisission's decision on Tuesday to approve the construction plans has hit the more than 11,000 Palestinians of Ras al-Amoud like a bombshell.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the Israeli move as a violation of his interim peace deals with Israel.

The future of East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed, is to be determined only in final-status peace talks which have yet to resume under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office in June.
Other Palestinian officials and Israeli peace activists also criticised the plan, which needs ministerial approval to be implemented, as a recipe for violence.

Israeli-Arab emotions over Jerusalem always run high. Israel's opening of a new entrance to a tourist tunnel close to Moslem holy sites in Jersualem ignited a wave of violence that killed 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis last September.
The new houses would sit on a 3.5 acre (1.4 hectare) plot in the heart of the Ras al-Amoud, just off the main road between East Jerusalem and the suburbs of Aizariyeh and Abu Dees.
A Miami-based Jewish businessman, Irving Moskowitz, known for his support of Jewish settlement activity in the West Bank, says he owns the land.
Palestinians say the land belongs to a prominent Arab family from East Jerusalem, which continues to claim the property.

The leftist Israeli Peace Now group says the construction plans are politically motivated. Palestinians accuse Israel of trying to block any return of East Jerusalem to Arab sovereignty in a permanent peace settlement.
Meanwhile, they fear that the Jewish presence would make their lives unbearable.

"This settlement will definitely stir problems in the area. It is common knowledge that wherever settlers move, they try to provoke confrontations with Palestinians. Just look at Hebron," said Abed al-Qawasmi, a 28-year-old merchant selling kitchenware a few hundred metres (yards) away from the controversial site.
"Wouldn't it be better if the municipality uses the land to build a park and a playground for the residents here instead of creating a source of friction?" Qawasmi said.

Palestinians say the housing plan represents a departure from Israeli policy, which had sought to ring Arab East Jerusalem with Jewish neighbourhoods but had largely avoided building Jewish homes in the heart of Arab areas of the city.
